extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and prosecuting reissue applications: when reissue claims are barred by the recapture doctrine, when broadened reissue claims are permitted or time-barred, and procedures for correcting inventorship by reissue (including oath/declaration requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recapture Category 1 — Omission of Surrender-Generating Limitation (recapture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue claims are broader by entirely omitting surrender-generating limitation(s) and are narrower in unrelated aspect(s): in this case, there is recapture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recapture exists because there is no addition of a new limitation that is related to the surrendered subject matter or if any new limitation related to the surrendered subject matter fails to materially narrow the claim (e.g., only adds what is known in the prior art). Example: original claims directed to ABC; reissue directed to ABD where C was a surrender-generating limitation (added or argued to obtain allowance). Eliminating C broadens into surrendered area; narrowing by D (unrelated to C) will not avoid recapture. See In re Clement, Pannu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recapture Category 2 — Broader in Unrelated Aspect(s), Narrower in Surrender Area (no recapture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue claims are narrower or equal in scope in the area related to surrendered subject matter and are broader in unrelated aspects: in this case, there is no recapture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: patent claimed ABCDE; reissue claims ABDE (omitting C) where a different limitation E was the surrender-generating limitation. Omitting C (unrelated to the surrender) and retaining/narrowing the surrender-generating limitation avoids recapture. Reissue can broaden in an aspect not germane to the prior-art rejection while narrowing in the area of surrender (e.g., narrow E to Especific). Also examples such as presenting AC or AB_broadC avoid recapture if they do not attempt to reclaim surrendered subject matter. See Mentor Corp. v. Coloplast; In re Clement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recapture Category 3 — Retain Surrender-Generating Limitation Unchanged (no recapture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue claims retain surrender-generating limitation(s) without change and are narrower or broader in unrelated aspects: there is no recapture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the limitation that led to surrender (e.g., C) remains unmodified in the reissue claims, changes elsewhere that do not affect the surrendered matter do not constitute recapture. Caveat: if applicant had previously argued that association of added limitation(s) defined over the art (synergy), then omission of either related limitation could be barred. See related discussion on surrender by argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recapture Category 4 — Retained but Broadened Surrender-Generating Limitation (may be recapture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue claims retain, in broadened form, the surrender-generating limitation(s): in this case there may be recapture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the retained limitation is broadened (e.g., C -> C_broadened) and that broadened limitation does not materially narrow the reissue claim relative to the original surrendered subject matter (for example, C_broadened is well-known in the prior art or was contained in prior art relied on), a recapture rejection can be made. If the modified limitation nevertheless 'materially narrows' relative to the original claim, recapture may be avoided. See In re Mostafazadeh; In re Youman; guidance that prior-art content used in original prosecution forms the ceiling for material narrowing analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Broadened Reissue Claim'
rubrics_metrics.description: A broadened reissue claim enlarges the scope of the claims of the original patent — i.e., is greater in scope than each and every claim of the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim is broadened if it is broader in at least one respect even though it may be narrower in other respects. A reissue claim that would cover any conceivable product or process that would not have infringed the original patent is broadened. Disclaimed claims (filed before reissue) are not part of the 'original patent' for this test. Case law examples: Vectra Fitness, Tillotson, In re Ruth, In re Rogoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-Year Filing Limit for Broadening Reissue (35 U.S.C. 251(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: No reissued patent shall be granted enlarging the scope of the claims of the original patent unless applied for within two years from the grant of the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broadened claim can be presented within two years from grant. If an intent to broaden is unequivocally indicated in a parent reissue application filed within two years, further broadened claims may be presented in continuation/divisional reissue applications after two years. A reissue filed on the two-year anniversary is timely. Case law: In re Staats, In re Graff, In re Fotland, In re Bennett, In re Doll. Use form ¶14.12 for improper broadened claims filed outside two years; examiner should identify claim limitations that broaden scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of Process or Article Claims (incl. computer-readable medium) Generally Broadening
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding process claims or article-of-manufacture claims (e.g., functional descriptive material on a computer-readable medium) in a reissue application is generally considered a broadening of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such additions must be applied for within two years of the grant of the original patent (or in an appropriate continuing reissue filed within two years). Example: converting patented process claims into corresponding article claims is generally broadening (Ex parte Wikdahl). See MPEP § 1412.03 and discussion of broadened claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent Claim Broadened but Not a Broadened Reissue Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim that is broadened in reissue is not a 'broadened reissue claim' if it remains narrower than or equal in scope to any other claim in the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because dependent claims incorporate limitations of the claims on which they depend, a dependent claim broadened relative to its patent form is not a broadened reissue claim so long as some other claim in the patent remains as broad as or broader than the reissued dependent claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: New Category of Invention Added in Reissue — Generally Broadening
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a new category of invention (e.g., adding method claims where only product claims existed) in a reissue application is generally considered broadening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, if the newly claimed method contains every limitation of the original claim(s) (so that infringement of the new claim necessarily results in infringement of the original claim), the addition may not be broadening. Examples and analysis guidance: Ex parte Wikdahl.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Rejection for Recapture — Use of Form ¶14.17 and Required Explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue claims that recapture surrendered subject matter should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 251 using form paragraph 14.17.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner Note: In bracket 2, the examiner should explain specifics of why recapture exists — identify omitted/broadened claim limitations that provide the 'broadening aspect', where in the original application the narrowed scope was presented/argued to obviate a rejection/objection, and that the reissue claim is not materially narrowed to avoid recapture. Explain the prima facie analysis for steps 1-3. See MPEP § 1412.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative Recapture Patterns (examples to be rejected)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common reissue claim patterns that should be rejected for recapture include: (1) eliminating the surrender-generating limitation; (2) eliminating the SGL and adding a narrowing limitation found not to be materially narrowing; (3) broadening the SGL where the broadened SGL is well known in the art; (4) broadening the SGL and adding another limitation that is not materially narrowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example shorthand patterns: 1) ABCD eliminates E (SGL). 2) ABCDF eliminates E and adds F which is not materially narrowing. 3) ABCDE broader: E_broader is well known in art. 4) ABCDE broader F: E_broader well known; add F not materially narrowing. Applicant can rebut patterns like 2 and 4 by showing added limitation F materially narrows with respect to surrendered subject matter; applicant should point out specifically which limitation is added and how it materially narrows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal Standard for Reissue Applicant — 'Materially Narrow' Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A reissue applicant may rebut a recapture rejection by demonstrating that the rejected claim includes one or more limitations that 'materially narrow' the reissue claims in a way that relates to the subject matter surrendered during original prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant should explicitly identify the added limitation(s) (e.g., limitation F) and explain how the limitation materially narrows the claims relative to what was surrendered. The examiner evaluates material narrowing relative to surrendered subject matter and prior art used in original prosecution (prior-art ceiling). See flowchart guidance referenced in MPEP § 1412.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath/Declaration Requirements for Broadening Reissue (filed on/after Sept 16, 2012)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any reissue application filed on or after Sept 16, 2012 must be applied for by all of the patentees; the original reissue oath/declaration in a broadening reissue must be signed by all inventors unless the original application was filed under 37 CFR 1.46 by the assignee of the entire interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For broadening reissue applications filed on/after Sept 16, 2012 the inventor’s oath/declaration must identify a specific claim that the application seeks to broaden (37 CFR 1.175(b)); a general statement that 'all claims are broadened' is insufficient. A supplemental oath/declaration is not needed for errors corrected subsequent to the original oath, but a replacement oath/declaration is needed where there was a failure to identify any error that would support reissue; replacement must be signed by all inventors unless original app was filed under 37 CFR 1.46 by an assignee. See MPEP § 1414.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath/Declaration Requirements for Broadening Reissue (filed before Sept 16, 2012)
rubrics_metrics.description: A broadening reissue application filed before Sept 16, 2012 must be applied for by all inventors — the reissue oath/declaration must be signed by all inventors and the error must have been made without deceptive intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a supplemental oath or declaration is needed to satisfy 37 CFR 1.175 in a pre-Sept 16, 2012 broadening reissue, it must be signed by all inventors. See In re Hayes and MPEP § 1414.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Certificate of Correction vs Reissue for Correcting Inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Correction of inventorship should normally be effected under 35 U.S.C. 256 and 37 CFR 1.324 (certificate of correction) when the only change is to correct inventorship; otherwise reissue under 35 U.S.C. 251 may be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the only change being made is to correct inventorship, request a certificate of correction (MPEP § 1481.02). Where 35 U.S.C. 256/37 CFR 1.324 do not apply, reissue is the appropriate vehicle. Reissue is available to correct misjoinder of inventors where 35 U.S.C. 256 is inadequate (Ex parte Scudder; A.F. Stoddard & Co. v. Dann).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue as Vehicle for Correcting Inventorship — Signature, Consent, and Procedural Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue may correct inventorship (35 U.S.C. 251) with specific requirements for the reissue oath/declaration and signatures, depending on whether the reissue seeks to enlarge claim scope and whether the original application was filed by an assignee under 37 CFR 1.46.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reissue does not seek to enlarge claim scope, the reissue oath may be made and sworn to by the assignee of the entire interest under 37 CFR 1.172. An assignee of part interest may not file unless other co-owners join or consent. If a named inventor X is to be deleted and has not assigned rights, X must consent to the reissue (37 CFR 1.172(a)). If inventors are required to sign and an inventor is being deleted, the deleted inventor need not sign; if an inventor is being added, the added inventor must sign the reissue oath/declaration. Where the original application was filed by the assignee under 37 CFR 1.46, the assignee may sign the oath/declaration for reissue filed on/after Sept 16, 2012; otherwise all inventors must sign unless 37 CFR 1.64 substitute statement applies (deceased, incapacitated, refuses, or cannot be found). Examples illustrate required signatures and substitute statements. See MPEP §§ 1412.04–1412.05 and 37 CFR 1.64/1.72/1.175.
